summary: Pupils (ages ~12–14) build fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr² and apply them to composite shapes with circular parts. The emphasis is on deriving both formulae from the meaning of π — the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3 — rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae. π is almost a definition of C = πd; A = πr² follows from cutting a circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae; both are eased by keeping each quantity's meaning and units in view (circumference is a length in cm, area is a covering in cm²).
misconceptions: Confusing radius and diameter — substituting the diameter where the radius is needed (or vice versa)
Swapping the circumference and area formulae (using πr² for circumference or 2πr for area)
Forgetting to square the radius, or squaring as 'doubling' (treating r² as 2r or as the diameter)
Giving an area in linear units, or a circumference in square units
On composite shapes, using the diameter as the radius of the semicircle, or dropping a straight edge from the perimeter

activities.title: Discover π by unrolling the circumference
steps: Take several circular objects (tins, lids, cups) of different sizes; wrap a string once around each and measure that length, then measure the diameter across each.

Divide each circumference by its diameter and record the result; notice the results are all close to the same value, a little over 3 (near π ≈ 3.14, allowing for small measurement errors), whatever the size of the circle.
Lay the measured circumference along a line marked off in lengths equal to that circle's own diameter, and see that it reaches to just past three diameters.
State in your own words: C = πd means the way round is 'a bit more than 3 diameters'.
activities.insight: π is the fixed ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14), so C = πd is almost a definition, not an arbitrary formula to recall.

activities.title: Build the area formula by rearranging wedges
steps: Cut a paper circle into a number of thin equal wedges (sectors) and fan them out, alternating points up and down, to form a shape close to a rectangle (parallelogram).
Identify the height of the near-rectangle as the radius r, and its length as half the way round the circle — half the circumference, which is πr.
Compute the area of the near-rectangle as length × height = πr × r = πr², and connect this to the circle's area.
Explain why cutting into more, thinner wedges makes the shape look more like a true rectangle.
activities.insight: A = πr² is a product of a length (πr) and a length (r) giving square units, derived from rearranging the circle — not a lookalike string to confuse with C = πd.

activities.title: Radius-or-diameter: check before you substitute
steps: For each problem, first write 'What am I given — radius or diameter?' and 'What does this formula need?' before substituting.
Given a diameter of 10 cm, find the area: halve it to get r = 5 cm, then compute A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (not π × 10²).
Given a radius of 5 cm, find both the circumference C = π × 10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm and the area A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
Investigate: if the radius doubles, what happens to the circumference and to the area? Confirm circumference doubles (×2) but area quadruples (×4).
activities.insight: Circumference uses d (or 2r) and area uses r²; you must convert a given diameter to a radius before using πr², and squaring is r × r (not doubling), so area grows with the square of the radius.

activities.title: Composite shapes: rectangle plus semicircle
steps: Take a composite shape — e.g. a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short (4 cm) end — and sketch it, labelling every given length.
Find the semicircle's radius as half its diameter (here r = 2 cm), not the full width.
For the area, add the rectangle's area to half the circle's area: 10 × 4 + ½ × π × 2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm².
For the perimeter, trace the actual boundary: include the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½ × π × diameter = ½ × π × 4 = 2π), with NO straight edge where the semicircle sits.
State the units: area in cm², perimeter in cm.
activities.insight: Composite shapes are decomposed into parts whose areas are added, while the perimeter follows the true outline — the arc replaces the covered straight edge, and the semicircle's radius is half its diameter.

activities.title: Formula-choice and unit checks (retrieval practice)
steps: Match each circle to its correct circumference and area expressions, watching for distractors that use πr² for circumference or 2πr for area.
Answer a question whose tempting wrong choice uses the diameter in πr² — reject it by halving to the radius first.
For each completed calculation, label the result with its unit and justify: a distance round is cm, a covering is cm².
Given a diameter, first find the radius before applying πr².
activities.insight: Keeping the two formulae distinct and attaching correct units (cm for circumference, cm² for area) consolidates the derived understanding, while converting a given diameter to a radius before using πr² guards the most common slip.

checkQuestion: Give the child a calculator and three tasks: (a) a circle with radius 5 cm — find its circumference and its area; (b) a circle given by its DIAMETER of 10 cm — find its area; (c) a composite shape: a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short end — find the perimeter and the area. Also ask them to explain, roughly, what π has to do with a circle. Watch whether they use the radius (not the diameter) in πr², whether they keep circumference and area formulae apart, whether they square rather than double the radius, and whether they use square units for area.
checkAnswer: (a) C = π×10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm². (b) radius = 5 cm, so A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (NOT π×10²). (c) perimeter = the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½×π×4 = 2π), with no straight edge where the semicircle sits; area = 10×4 + ½×π×2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm². π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3. Circumference in cm, area in cm².
